messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Bao returned to his university campus in September looking like a ghost of the energetic student who had left in May. The 22-year-old had spent his summer as a relief worker, a role he had seen as a vital expression of his values. But the experience had hollowed him out. The trauma occurred during what was supposed to be a routine food and water distribution at a makeshift checkpoint. Bao was handing supplies to a young family when two soldiers in crisp uniforms approached. He remembered the feeling of their eyes on him, a flat, indifferent surveillance that made the hair on his arms stand up. They spoke to the father in a language Bao didn't understand, and then, with sudden, brutal efficiency, they grabbed the man. Bao tried to intervene, citing his status as a neutral aid worker, but one of the soldiers shoved him back so hard he stumbled and fell. He could do nothing but watch as the family was separated and the man was dragged away. The entire time, he felt the weight of the crowd's gaze, a silent testament to his powerlessness.

Now, back in the familiar environment of his American university, this sense of powerlessness has become the lens through which he sees the world. Bao has come to believe he is fundamentally helpless, that he failed in the single most important role he ever had. This deeply held conviction fuels a relentless, exhausting vigilance. As he walks across campus, he is no longer a student heading to class but a target scanning for threats. His perception of his surroundings has been warped by the certainty that danger is imminent; he is constantly monitoring for the presence of authority figures and feels a prickling sense of dread whenever he thinks someone might be watching him. The open, friendly campus of his memory has transformed into a landscape of potential threats that he must navigate with extreme caution.

This state of high alert means that triggers are everywhere. Last week, while walking toward the main library, he saw two campus police officers standing near the entrance. The sight of their dark blue uniforms was an instant, physical blow. It wasn't just fear that seized him, but a crushing wave of shame that confirmed his most damning self-appraisal: *I have failed*. His heart began to pound violently, a familiar and hated response that made him feel as though his own body was his enemy, still screaming of danger in a place that should be safe. The physiological panic cemented his belief that he was broken beyond repair. In that moment, overwhelmed by the internal cacophony of fear and self-loathing, he abruptly turned away, changing his route to avoid the uniformed officers. He ducked his head, pretending to read a text, and began a long, circuitous walk around the back of the building, his breath coming in short, sharp gasps.

This pattern of reacting to triggers with immediate avoidance has, over the past few months, systematically dismantled his life. He now plans his entire day around avoiding any potential encounter with campus security, which means he has stopped going to the student union entirely. He no longer meets up with the friends he socialised with before the trip, terrified of making eye contact and having them see the failure he feels etched onto his face. His world has shrunk to the path between his dorm room and his lecture halls, a route he walks with his eyes fixed firmly on the ground. The isolation has become profound. It was the threat of this collapse spreading to his academic life—the prospect of failing his classes and proving his helplessness once and for all—that finally pushed him to seek help. He arrived at the clinic not with any real hope for recovery, but with the quiet desperation of someone who is terrified he is right about himself and is running out of places to hide.
